rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted for a single connection. When the login failure counter reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the login failure are written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. Although the recommended value is 4, set the number according to site policy.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep maxauthtries

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through user .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted. This option applies only to SSH protocol version 2.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep hostbasedauthentication

rules.title: SSH root login is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user can log in via ssh. The default is "no".
rules.impact: Disallowing root login via SSH requires system administrators to authenticate using their individual accounts and then escalate to root via sudo or su. This in turn limits the ability to deny authorship and provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep permitrootlogin

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with ssh.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep ignorerhosts

rules.title: The usb-storage/usb-storage.ko kernel service/module is disabled
rules.explanation: With automounting enabled, any user with physical access to a USB drive on the machine can obtain a means to transfer and store files, which may lead to malware propagation.
rules.impact: Restricting USB access on the system reduces the likelihood of device-based attacks and reduces possible malware introduction vectors.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var /tmp is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion if it is not bound to a separate partition. In addition, giving /var/tmp its own file system allows the administrator to set the noexec option on the mount, making /var/tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. Once the program is updated, the hard link is broken and the attacker has their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability is found in the program, the attacker can continue to exploit the known flaw.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The noexec parameter is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot execute files from /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to ensure that system logs are stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because logs can become quite large) and protection of audit data.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to Ensure that data collected by auditd is stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because the audit.log file can become quite large) and protection of audit data. The audit daemon calculates how much free space remains and takes action based on the results. If other processes (for example, syslog) consume space on the same partition as auditd, it may not operate as intended.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home is configured
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to support disk storage for local users.
rules.impact: If the system is intended to support local users, create a separate partition for the /home directory to protect against resource exhaustion and to limit the types of files that can be stored in /home.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /home partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because user partitions are not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices.

rules.title: Use only approved MAC algorithms
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the MAC algorithm types that SSH may use during communication.
rules.impact: MD5 algorithms and 96-bit MACs are considered weak and have been shown to increase vulnerability to SSH downgrade attacks. Weak algorithms continue to receive significant attention as a weakness that can be exploited with advanced computing capability. An attacker who breaks the algorithm may use a MiTM position to decrypt the SSH tunnel and obtain credentials and information.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep -i "MACs"

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep clientaliveinterval

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to present environment options to the ssh daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path in which ssh executes Trojan programs).
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep permituserenvironment

rules.title: The sticky bit is set on all world-writable directories is configured
rules.explanation: Setting the sticky bit on world-writable directories (such as /tmp) prevents users from deleting or renaming files in that directory that they do not own.
rules.impact: This feature prevents deletion or renaming of files in world-writable directories (for example, /tmp) that are owned by another user.
rules.scope: Sticky bit value of all world-writable files

rules.title: The usb-storage/usb-storage.ko kernel service/module is disabled
rules.explanation: With automounting enabled, any user with physical access to a USB drive on the machine can obtain a means to transfer and store files, which may lead to malware propagation.
rules.impact: Restricting USB access on the system reduces the likelihood of device-based attacks and reduces possible malware introduction vectors.

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep banner

rules.title: A password is set for the bootloader (GRUB) is configured
rules.explanation: A bootloader password prevents unauthorized changes to boot parameters and modification of the kernel/bootloader parameters with physical/local access.
rules.impact: The absence of a bootloader password allows an attacker to change kernel parameters (for example, disable AppArmor/SELinux) and bypass protections.

rules.title: Permissions and ownership of bootloader configuration files are restricted is configured
rules.explanation: Access to bootloader configuration files must be restricted (root-only) to prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow a local user to change boot parameters and potentially bypass security mechanisms.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is set to 1 or less is configured
rules.explanation: Restricting ptrace (ptrace_scope) prevents unsafe access between processes of different users.
rules.impact: Disabled or unrestricted ptrace may allow local users to interfere with other users' processes (a key privileged access risk).

rules.title: ASLR is enabled (kernel.randomize_va_space = 2)
rules.explanation: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) makes it harder to predict stack/library locations, which complicates exploitation of buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Disabled ASLR significantly simplifies successful exploitation of vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Core dumps are either disabled or that their permissions and storage location are secure (ulimit -c 0 or /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) is configured
rules.explanation: Core dumps may contain sensitive data (passwords, keys). Restricting core file generation and permissions prevents disclosure of confidential information.
rules.impact: Unlimited core dumps increase the risk of secret data leakage when processes crash.

rules.title: /etc/motd contains an appropriate warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd (message of the day) file informs users of the acceptable use policy and warns of legal restrictions.
rules.impact: Absence of warning banners may weaken the legal position in incidents and reduce user awareness.

rules.title: /etc/motd contains an appropriate warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd (message of the day) file informs users of the acceptable use policy and warns of legal restrictions.
rules.impact: Absence of warning banners may weaken the legal position in incidents and reduce user awareness.

rules.title: The local banner is configured in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: A local banner (for example /etc/issue) provides a warning to users when logging in via the console.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner does not create a technical vulnerability, but it reduces user awareness and legal protection.

rules.title: The local banner is configured in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: A local banner (for example /etc/issue) provides a warning to users when logging in via the console.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner does not create a technical vulnerability, but it reduces user awareness and legal protection.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net contains a correct banner is configured
rules.explanation: The remote access banner (for example, /etc/issue.net) informs remote users of the rules and warns against unauthorized access.
rules.impact: As with the local banner, its absence reduces legal protection and user awareness.

rules.title: /etc/motd is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file must be owned by root and be read-only to prevent unauthorized banner modification.
rules.impact: A modified banner may mislead users or conceal important messages.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to be enabled at boot and ensure that it has not been overridden by GRUB boot parameters.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot in your GRUB configuration to ensure that the controls it provides will not be overridden.
rules.scope: The SELINUX parameter in /etc/selinux/config; the selinux and enforcing parameters in /etc/default/grub

rules.title: The SELinux state is enforcing is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can be in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, enforcing. Enforcing is the recommended default operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux applies the loaded security policy to the entire system. Permissive - the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful for SELinux policy development. Disabled is strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot time to ensure that the controls it provides are continuously in effect.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and function as a message of the day for authenticated users. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log in on local terminals. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information may be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured services. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at logon. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following parameters, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/motd are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after logon and function as the message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/issue are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on to local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/issue.net are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue.net does not have the correct owner, it can be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed is configured
rules.explanation: Patches are periodically released for installed software either due to security flaws or to add additional functionality.
rules.impact: Newer patches may contain security improvements that will not be available after the latest full update. As a result, it is recommended to use the most recent software patches to take advantage of the newest functionality. As with any software installation, organizations need to determine whether a given update meets their requirements and verify compatibility and support of any additional software with the selected update version.

rules.title: Xinetd is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: EXtended InterNET Daemon (xinetd) is an open-source super-daemon that replaced the original inetd daemon. The xinetd daemon listens for well-known services and launches the appropriate daemon to correctly respond to service requests.
rules.impact: If xinetd services are not required, it is recommended to disable the daemon.

rules.title: Time synchronization is used is configured
rules.explanation: System time should be synchronized among all systems in the environment. This is typically done by establishing an authoritative time server or set of servers, and all systems synchronize their clocks to them.
rules.impact: Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos, and also ensures that log files have consistent timestamps across the enterprise, which aids forensic investigations.

rules.title: NTP is configured
rules.explanation: Ntp is a daemon that implements the Network Time Protocol (NTP). It is intended to synchronize system clocks across different systems and to use a source that is highly accurate. NTP can be configured as a client and/or a server. This recommendation applies only if ntp is used on the system.
rules.impact: If ntp is used on the system, proper configuration is vital to ensure correct operation of time synchronization.

rules.title: Compliance with the requirement: NTP_conf is configured
rules.explanation: Requirement: NTP_conf. This check belongs to the secure configuration profile.
rules.impact: Failure to meet the requirement reduces system security and may increase the attack surface.

rules.title: Chrony is configured
rules.explanation: Chrony is a daemon that implements the Network Time Protocol (NTP), intended to synchronize system clocks across various systems and use a source that is highly accurate. chrony can be configured as a client and/or a server.
rules.impact: If the system uses chrony, correct configuration is vital to ensure time synchronization operates properly. This recommendation applies only if the system uses chrony.

rules.title: Compliance with the requirement: Chrony_ is configured
rules.explanation: Requirement: Chrony_. The check applies to the secure configuration profile.
rules.impact: Failure to meet the requirement reduces system security and may increase the attack surface.

rules.title: The X Window System is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface (GUI) in which users can have multiple windows in which to run programs and various add-ons. The X Window System is typically used on workstations where users log on, but not on servers where users typically do not log on using a graphical interface.
rules.impact: If your organization does not require graphical login via X Windows, remove it to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The Avahi server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a system for multicast DNS/DNS-SD service discovery. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on a local network without a specific configuration. For example, a user can connect a computer to the network and Avahi will automatically find printers to print to, files to browse, people to communicate with, and network services running on the machine.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is generally not required for system functionality. It is recommended to disable the service to reduce the potential likelihood of attack.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Talk client is a legacy program for network chat.
rules.impact: Legacy talk protocols do not encrypt data and are vulnerable to interception.

rules.title: Telnet is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Telnet client may be used to access insecure server services.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits logins and passwords in cleartext.

rules.title: Ldap-utils is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: If LDAP is not used in the infrastructure, its client packages should be removed to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Unused LDAP increases the number of dependencies and vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The FTP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows networked computers to transfer files between a server and clients over a network where authentication is absent (disallow anonymous user connections to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or credentials. It is recommended to use sftp if file transfer is required. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The FTP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows networked computers to transfer files between a server and clients over a network where authentication is absent (disallow anonymous user connections to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or credentials. It is recommended to use sftp if file transfer is required. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The TFTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: The absence of IMAP and POP3 servers is configured
rules.explanation: IMAP and POP3 servers (dovecot-imapd, dovecot-pop3d) should not be installed unless required for operation.
rules.impact: These protocols are obsolete and vulnerable to attacks if not configured properly.

rules.title: Unused IMAP and POP3 server is not disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Dovecot is an open-source IMAP and POP3 server for Linux-based systems used by default.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Samba is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise filesystems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and filesystems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this service can be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The HTTP proxy server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: If a proxy server is not required, it is recommended to disable the squid proxy to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The SNMP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP, execute commands, or collect information and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: An SNMP server can communicate using SNMP v1, which transmits data in the clear and does not require authentication to execute commands. If at all possible, it is recommended that the SNMP service not be used. If SNMP is required, the server should be configured to prohibit the use of SNMP v1.

rules.title: Dnsmasq is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The dnsmasq DNS server must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DNS server may be used for "DNS cache poisoning" attacks.

rules.title: The Telnet server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems via the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow a user with access to network traffic analysis to steal credentials.

rules.title: NFS and RPC are not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most common file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides the ability for systems to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not export NFS shares or act as an NFS client, it is recommended to disable these services to reduce the likelihood of a remote attack.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The rsh package contains client commands for rsh services.
rules.impact: These legacy clients contain numerous vulnerabilities and have been replaced by the more secure SSH package. Even if the server is removed, it is best to ensure that the client is also removed to prevent users from accidentally using these commands.

rules.title: Requirement compliance: Telnet.socket is configured
rules.explanation: Requirement: Telnet.socket. The check applies to the secure configuration profile.
rules.impact: Failure to meet the requirement reduces system security and may increase the attack surface.

rules.title: Time synchronization is configured in /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/chrony.conf
rules.explanation: Time synchronization is important for audit and logging.
rules.impact: Inconsistent time causes audit errors and log desynchronization.

rules.title: Chrony is not run as the root user is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/sysconfig/chronyd file allows configuration of parameters for chrony, including the user under which chrony runs. By default this is the chrony user.
rules.impact: Services must not be configured to run as the root user.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Use of unencrypted MEDIUM transmission may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a method for looking up information from a central database.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended that the software be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Source-routed packets allow the sender to specify the path and bypass filters.
rules.impact: Accepting such packets enables routing and filtering bypass.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages can be used to redirect traffic to an attacker.
rules.impact: Accepting redirect packets allows traffic interception.

rules.title: Source routed packets are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: In a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. Conversely, packets that are not source-routed follow a path determined by routers on the network. In some cases, systems may not be routable or reachable from certain locations (for example, private addresses versus Internet-routable addresses), and source-routed packets would therefore need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system's acceptance of source-routed packets. If source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to the system's private addresses because a route can be specified rather than relying on routing protocols that would not permit that routing.
rules.scope: The parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route or net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host information for sending packets via an alternate path. This is a way to update your system's routing tables from outside. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.
rules.impact: Attackers can use forged ICMP redirect messages to maliciously alter system routing tables and cause them to send packets to the wrong networks and allow captured system packets.
rules.scope: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects parameters, or net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects, in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Some TCP/IP implementations generate responses to broadcast ICMP requests with incorrect error codes. Ignoring such responses protects against network scanning.
rules.impact: Without filtering spoofed ICMP replies, a server can be used to amplify attacks and network scanning. Incorrect ICMP messages may also disclose network topology information.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Responses to ICMP echo broadcast requests (Smurf attacks) can be used to amplify DDoS. Ignoring such requests prevents the server from participating in such attacks.
rules.impact: If the server responds to broadcast ICMP requests, an attacker can use it as an amplifier in a Smurf DDoS attack, generating traffic 500–1000 times the original.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects can modify the kernel routing table. Accepting them from arbitrary hosts creates a vector for route poisoning attacks.
rules.impact: An attacker on the network can send spoofed ICMP redirects to change the server's traffic routing through their node. This is the basis of MITM attacks at the network layer.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are accepted only from default gateways. Even this restriction does not guarantee protection, because a gateway may be compromised or spoofed.
rules.impact: Even secure ICMP redirects can be used by an attacker who has compromised the default gateway to alter server traffic routing for a MITM attack.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Reverse Path Filtering (RPF) drops packets with a source IP address that is not reachable via the incoming interface. This is protection against IP spoofing.
rules.impact: Without RPF, an attacker can send packets with spoofed source IP addresses. This is used to bypass ACLs, implement blind TCP attacks, and spoof addresses in network attacks.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: IP source routing allows the sender to specify the packet path. This obsolete feature is used exclusively for attacks and must be disabled on all modern systems.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets allow an attacker to bypass firewalls and routing systems by forcing traffic through nodes they control for interception or modification.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged is configured
rules.explanation: Logging martian packets with impossible source addresses helps detect IP spoofing attempts and network anomalies. This is an important security monitoring capability.
rules.impact: Without logging of suspicious packets, IP-spoofing attacks and scans from forged addresses remain invisible. This substantially hinders intrusion detection and incident investigation.

rules.title: DCCP is disabled
rules.explanation: Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport-layer protocol that supports streaming multimedia and telephony. DCCP provides a way to access congestion control without needing to do so at the application layer, but it does not provide unordered delivery.
rules.impact: If the protocol is not required, it is recommended not to install drivers in order to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: SCTP is disabled
rules.explanation: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport-layer protocol used to support message exchange with multiple message streams in a single connection. It performs functions similar to TCP and UDP, including features of both: it is message-oriented like UDP and provides reliable sequential message transport with congestion control like TCP.
rules.impact: If the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module and to disable the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Iptables is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Iptables is a utility that allows a system administrator to configure tables provided by the Linux kernel firewall, implemented as various Netfilter modules, as well as the chains and rules it stores.
rules.impact: Iptables is required to manage and configure the firewall.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter determines how to handle an audit log file that reaches the maximum size. The keep_logs value will rotate logs but never delete old logs.
rules.impact: It is important that an appropriate log file size is defined so that logs do not impact the system and audit data is not lost.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.

rules.explanation: Configure the maximum audit log file size. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is started.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the benefits of maintaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing audit history.

rules.impact: Collection of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.impact: Legacy MD5/DES methods provide weak password protection.

rules.title: SSH access is configured
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups directives restrict which users are permitted SSH access. This implements the principle of least privilege for remote logon.
rules.impact: Without an explicit restriction, all system accounts, including service accounts, have SSH access. Compromise of any account provides a remote logon path and further persistence.

rules.title: The sshd banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH banner displays a warning before authentication.
rules.impact: A legal warning before logon may assist in legal proceedings.

rules.title: Sshd ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: Configure modern cryptographic algorithms for SSH.
rules.impact: Protection against outdated and insecure encryption algorithms.

rules.title: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: Control SSH session inactivity timeout.
rules.impact: Preventing hanging sessions and conserving resources.

rules.title: GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: Disable authentication via GSSAPI.
rules.impact: Simplifying configuration and removing unnecessary dependencies.

rules.title: Root can log in only via console or SSH with a key is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/securetty file must contain only valid terminals for root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized root access increases the escalation risk.

rules.title: SSH version 2 is used is configured
rules.explanation: SSH supports two different incompatible protocols: SSH1 and SSH2. SSH1 was the original protocol and was subject to security problems. SSH2 is more advanced and secure.
rules.impact: SSH v1 is susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, unlike SSH v2.

rules.title: Re-authentication on privilege elevation is not disabled globally is configured
rules.explanation: The global !authenticate flag in sudoers disables authentication for all users. This completely undermines the sudo security mechanism.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication means that any user can obtain root privileges without entering a password. Capture of any user session immediately results in full system compromise.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this will enable PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in the /etc/pam.d/su file, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead allows system administrators to better control user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through user .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted. This option applies only to SSH protocol version 2.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits authentication with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote shell access to accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to present environment options to the ssh daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path in which ssh executes Trojan programs).

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with ssh.

rules.title: SSH X11 forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The X11Forwarding parameter provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic over the connection to enable remote graphical sessions.
rules.impact: Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that remote X11 servers of users who logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding may be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note that even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always set up their own forwarding servers.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not overridden is configured
rules.explanation: The system-wide cryptographic policy can be overridden or disabled for OpenSSH.
rules.impact: Overriding or opting out of the system-wide crypto policy may allow use of less secure ciphers, MACs, KexAlgorithms, and GSSAPIKexAlgorithm.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted for a single connection. When the login failure counter reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the login failure are written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. Although the recommended value is 4, set the number according to site policy.

rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more unauthenticated connections may remain open. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a smaller value for LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.

rules.explanation: NOPASSWD in sudoers disables the password requirement when executing privileged commands. Such entries must be excluded because they violate the principle of identity confirmation.
rules.impact: Without a password requirement, an attacker who obtains access to a user session (terminal hijacking, a compromised SSH key) immediately obtains full root privileges without an additional barrier.

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.

rules.explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the maximum password lifetime. A value of 365 days or less ensures regular password rotation and limits the impact of password compromise.
rules.impact: Without an expiration, a password may remain unchanged for years. A compromised password gives an attacker persistent access with no automatic revocation mechanism.

rules.title: The minimum password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The minimum password age defines the number of days a password must be used before it can be changed. PASS_MIN_DAYS <N> is the minimum number of days allowed between password changes. Any attempt to change the password before this time will be rejected. If not specified, 0 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe the chosen password is protected against compromise. Unfortunately, passwords are compromised, and if an attacker targets a specific individual user's account, then, with prior knowledge about that user, reuse of old, potentially compromised passwords may lead to a security breach. By restricting how frequently a password can be changed, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls.
rules.scope: See section 5.5.1.1 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: The password expiration warning days are configured

rules.impact: Without timely warnings, users may be caught by surprise by password expiration and locked out. Unplanned lockouts often lead to the use of insecure recovery procedures.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured

rules.impact: Accounts with expired passwords that are not locked out automatically remain on the system with outdated (potentially weak) passwords. Abandoned accounts are a common vector for unauthorized access.

rules.title: Default user umask value
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). Umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. Users who want their files and directories to be readable by other users by default may choose a different default umask by inserting a umask command into the standard shell configuration files (.profile, .bashrc, etc.) in their home directories.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask ensures that users make a conscious choice regarding file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: User shell timeout
rules.explanation: TMOUT by default defines the shell idle timeout for users. The TMOUT value is measured in seconds.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access to another user's shell session that has been left unattended. It also terminates an idle session and frees resources associated with that session.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set to legacy is configured
