rules.impact: If the system-wide Legacy crypto policy is selected, it includes support for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and SSH2 or later. DSA, 3DES, and RC4 algorithms are allowed, while RSA and Diffie-Hellman parameters are accepted if they are greater than 1023 bits. These legacy protocols and algorithms can make the system vulnerable to attacks, including those listed in RFC 7457.

rules.title: The rsync service is not installed or is masked is configured
rules.explanation: The rsync service must not be active unless required for operations.
rules.impact: Rsync may expose files if configured incorrectly.

rules.title: Auditd is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Capturing system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: Auditd is enabled in grub
rules.explanation: Configure grub2 so that auditable processes can be audited even if they start before auditd starts.
rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before audit so that potentially malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel-level audit subsystem uses a socket buffer queue to store audit events. Whenever a new audit event arrives, it is recorded and prepared for addition to this queue. The kernel boot parameter audit_backlog_limit=N, where N represents the number of messages, ensures that the queue cannot grow beyond a certain size. If an audit event is recorded that would cause the queue to exceed this limit, a failure occurs that is handled according to the system configuration.
rules.impact: If an audit event is recorded that causes the queue to grow beyond audit_backlog_limit, a failure occurs, audit records are lost, and potentially malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit=1 parameter is present in the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX line of /etc/default/grub is configured
rules.explanation: To avoid losing events that occur before auditd starts, enable audit=1 in the kernel parameters.
rules.impact: Without early auditing, actions before auditd starts cannot be traced.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is set to at least 8192 in the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit parameter defines the size of the audit event buffer during kernel boot, before the auditd daemon starts. An insufficient buffer size results in loss of early-boot events.
rules.impact: A low backlog value results in loss of audit data.

rules.title: Space_left_action is set to halt or single in /etc/audit/auditd.conf is configured
rules.explanation: If log storage is full, the system should halt safely to prevent loss of events.
rules.impact: Ignoring log overflow leads to loss of audit data and concealment of attacks.

rules.title: Correct logrotate rotation is configured for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: Log rotation prevents overflow and preserves event history.
rules.impact: Without rotation, the file system may fill up.

rules.title: The last line of audit.rules contains -e 2 is configured
rules.explanation: Immutability of audit rules prevents an attacker from modifying them while the system is running.
rules.impact: Modifiable rules allow an attacker to conceal their actions.

rules.title: Auditd rules for programs with setuid and/or setgid are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor privileged programs that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution to determine whether unprivileged users are executing these commands.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: System calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes.
rules.impact: Tracking these calls from unprivileged users can provide the system administrator with evidence that improper deletion of files and file attributes associated with protected files is occurring. Although this audit option will capture all events, system administrators will want to look for specific privileged files that are deleted or modified.

rules.title: Auditd rules for sudoers are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system has been correctly configured to force system administrators to log in as themselves first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, scope changes can be monitored. The /etc/sudoers file or files in /etc/sudoers.d will be written when the files or related attributes are changed. Audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".
rules.impact: Changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d may indicate that an unauthorized change was made to the system administrator's scope of activity.

rules.title: System administrator commands (sudo) are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo grants users temporary elevated privileges to perform operations. Monitor the administrator with temporary elevated privileges and the operations they perform.
rules.impact: Creating an audit log of administrators with temporarily elevated privileges and the operations they performed is essential for reporting. Administrators will want to correlate events recorded in the audit trail with entries recorded in the sudo log file to verify that unauthorized commands were not executed.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog software is recommended in environments where journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: Rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transport (that is, TCP), the ability to log in database format, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: ForwardToSyslog=yes is set in /etc/systemd/journald.conf is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd-journald should forward logs to rsyslog for centralized storage and rotation.
rules.impact: Without forwarding, logs may be lost when the journal is cleared.

rules.title: Password policies are set to minlen 14 and that character classes (upper, lower, digits, others) are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/pwquality.conf file defines minimum password length and complexity.
rules.impact: Weak password requirements make passwords easy to guess.

rules.title: Deny 5 and unlock_time 900 are set in /etc/security/faillock.conf is configured
rules.explanation: The faillock mechanism locks an account after several failed logon attempts.
rules.impact: Without restrictions, password brute-force is possible.

rules.title: The pam_wheel module is enabled in /etc/pam.d/su to restrict use of su
rules.explanation: The su command must be allowed only for members of the wheel or sudo group.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su access increases the risk of unauthorized root logon.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, the public key is the key that can be used to verify digital signatures generated using the corresponding private key. Only the public key corresponding to the private key will be able to successfully authenticate.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

rules.title: Only strong ciphers are used is configured
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the ciphers that SSH may use during communication.
rules.impact: Weak ciphers used for authentication in a cryptographic module cannot guarantee confidentiality or integrity, and system data may be compromised.

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is set to one minute or less
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more unauthenticated connections may remain open. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a smaller value for LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.

rules.title: PASS_MAX_DAYS does not exceed 365 in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: Regular password changes reduce the risk of compromise.
rules.impact: Unlimited password lifetime increases the risk of compromise.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in /etc/pam.d/su, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead gives system administrators better control over user privilege elevation for privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can record only that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: No /etc/shadow entries have an empty password field is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow must not contain empty password fields.
rules.impact: An empty password field allows logon without authentication.

rules.title: /etc/group contains no lines starting with the '+' character is configured
rules.explanation: "+" in /etc/group indicates a legacy NIS binding.
rules.impact: May result in unintended group membership.

rules.title: All GIDs specified in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Every group specified in /etc/passwd must exist in /etc/group.
rules.impact: A nonexistent group causes access control problems.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist in /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: UID must be unique for each user.
rules.impact: Duplicate UIDs allow users to act on behalf of others.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Group names must be unique to avoid confusion in access rights and group policy control.
rules.impact: Duplicate group names make security management more difficult.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Over time, errors and system administration changes can result in groups being defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group.
rules.impact: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group permissions are not properly controlled.

rules.title: Users' dot files are not group- or world-writable is configured
rules.explanation: Although a system administrator can set secure permissions on users' dot files, users can easily override them.
rules.impact: Group-writable or world-writable user configuration files can allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate user identifier (UID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure proper access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem type is a compressed, read-only Linux filesystem embedded in small systems. A cramfs image can be used without first decompressing it.
rules.impact: Removing support for unnecessary file system types reduces the local system attack surface.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs file system is a free implementation of the Veritas file system and is not used on typical Debian servers.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the risk of exploiting drivers and untrusted kernel code.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: HFS is a legacy Apple file system. It is rarely needed on Linux servers and may contain unused code.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the potential attack surface in legacy modules.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: HFS+ (hfsplus) is used on macOS but is rarely used on Debian servers. Unnecessary modules should be disabled.
rules.impact: Disabling reduces the risk of loading unnecessary drivers and attacks via their vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: JFFS2 is intended for flash memory on embedded devices, is not used on servers, and represents unnecessary code in the kernel.
rules.impact: The presence of the unused JFFS2 kernel module increases the attack surface and creates a risk of exploiting vulnerabilities in its code.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: OverlayFS is used to overlay filesystems (container scenarios). If it is not required, it is better to disable it to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces risk, especially if the system does not use containers that depend on overlayfs.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage module allows connecting USB storage devices.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the risk of data leakage and malware spread from external media.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /home in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid prevents execution of setuid/setgid programs from /home, reducing the risk of local privilege escalation.
rules.impact: If nosuid is absent, user-owned setuid binaries may be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev on /var prevents special device files from being created by processes writing to /var.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of exploitation via special files in /var.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid on /var prevents execution of setuid/setgid programs placed under /var (for example, log/ftp directories).
rules.impact: If nosuid is missing, exploits via setuid binaries placed in /var are possible.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prohibits creation of special devices in the log directory, which prevents possible security bypasses.
rules.impact: Absence of nodev provides an additional attack vector via special files.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid protects logs from hosting setuid programs, which could potentially lead to privilege escalation.
rules.impact: This reduces the likelihood that logs will be used as storage for setuid binaries.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec reduces the risk of running scripts/binaries directly from /var/log.
rules.impact: Absence of this control may allow execution of code placed in logs by an attacker.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prevents creation of special devices in the audit log directory, protecting their integrity.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of compromising audit files via special devices.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid protects audit logs from hosting setuid programs, which could distort audit data.
rules.impact: Maintaining log integrity is critical for forensics and monitoring.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec prevents execution of code from the audit log directory, preserving log integrity.
rules.impact: This reduces the likelihood that logs will be used to execute malicious code.

rules.title: The repo_gpgcheck parameter is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The repo_gpgcheck parameter, located in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and in individual /etc/yum.repos.d/* files, verifies the GPG signature of repository data (repodata).
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the repository data signature is always verified before installation to guarantee that the software has not been tampered with in any way.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce or complain mode is configured
rules.explanation: All loaded AppArmor profiles should be active — either in enforce mode (restrictions are applied) or complain mode (violations are logged). Inactive profiles provide no protection.
rules.impact: A profile in unconfined mode does not restrict the application, which completely negates AppArmor protection. A compromised application without a profile has access to all system resources.

rules.title: Permissions and ownership of bootloader configuration files are restricted is configured
rules.explanation: Access to bootloader configuration files must be restricted (root-only) to prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow a local user to change boot parameters and potentially bypass security mechanisms.

rules.title: /etc/motd contains an appropriate warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd (message of the day) file informs users of the acceptable use policy and warns of legal restrictions.
rules.impact: Absence of warning banners may weaken the legal position in incidents and reduce user awareness.

rules.title: The local banner is configured in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: A local banner (for example /etc/issue) provides a warning to users when logging in via the console.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner does not create a technical vulnerability, but it reduces user awareness and legal protection.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net contains a correct banner is configured
rules.explanation: The remote access banner (for example, /etc/issue.net) informs remote users of the rules and warns against unauthorized access.
rules.impact: As with the local banner, its absence reduces legal protection and user awareness.

rules.title: /etc/motd is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file must be owned by root and be read-only to prevent unauthorized banner modification.
rules.impact: A modified banner may mislead users or conceal important messages.

rules.title: /etc/issue is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file must be protected from modification by ordinary users so that banners remain trustworthy.
rules.impact: Altering the banner reduces trust and may conceal security warnings.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: Protecting /etc/issue.net ensures that remote banners are not modified by unauthorized persons.
rules.impact: An untrusted banner may mislead remote users and serve as a social engineering vector.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables EtM for ssh is configured
rules.explanation: Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM). Ciphertext is generated by encrypting plaintext and then appending a MAC of the encrypted plaintext.
rules.impact: There is an effective attack against the use of SSH Cipher-Block-Chaining (CBC) with Encrypt-then-MAC, as described in CVE-2023-48795.

rules.title: The disable-user-list option in GDM is enabled
rules.explanation: This option hides the user list on the logon screen.
rules.impact: Hiding the user list makes credential guessing more difficult.

rules.title: GDM screen lock on idle is configured
rules.explanation: The screen must lock after a period of inactivity.
rules.impact: This prevents unauthorized access if the user steps away.

rules.title: Prohibit canceling GDM screen lock
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to override the screen lock.
rules.impact: This makes bypassing protections more difficult.

rules.title: Automatic mounting of removable media in GDM is disabled
rules.explanation: USB device automounting can be dangerous.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of executing malicious code from removable media.

rules.title: Prohibit overriding the disablement of automount in GDM
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to enable automounting.
rules.impact: Maintaining a stable security configuration.

rules.title: The autorun-never option in GDM is enabled
rules.explanation: This option prevents autorun of removable media contents.
rules.impact: Prevents execution of malicious code when devices are connected.

rules.title: Prohibit overriding autorun-never in GDM
rules.explanation: Users must not be able to disable this option.
rules.impact: Provides persistent protection against autorun.

rules.title: XDMCP is disabled
rules.explanation: XDCMP allows remote control of X11 sessions.
rules.impact: Disabling this prevents potential remote access attacks.

rules.title: Legacy time services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Legacy time TCP/UDP services (not ntpd/chrony) are not required.
rules.impact: Use of legacy time protocols introduces authentication risks.

rules.title: Rsh (rlogin, rexec) is disabled
rules.explanation: RSH/Rlogin are legacy remote access services without encryption.
rules.impact: Use of r-services provides full unencrypted remote access.

rules.title: Web proxy services are not in use is configured
rules.explanation: Squid is an HTTP proxy. If proxy functionality is not required, Squid should be removed so it does not create an unauthorized path to the Internet.
rules.impact: An unauthorized proxy allows users and malware to bypass web traffic controls and filtering. It may be used for covert outbound connections.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only delivery
rules.explanation: The MTA (postfix, sendmail) must accept mail only from localhost (127.0.0.1/::1). Listening on external interfaces turns the server into an open mail relay.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be used as an open relay for sending spam or phishing email. In addition, it exposes attack surface on mail protocols.

rules.title: Telnet is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Telnet client may be used to access insecure server services.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits logins and passwords in cleartext.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use is configured
rules.explanation: Accurate time synchronization is critical for correct Kerberos operation, TLS certificates, audit logs, and distributed systems. Exactly one NTP daemon must be running.
rules.impact: Time desynchronization breaks Kerberos authentication (±5 minute tolerance), makes timestamps in logs unreliable for incident investigation, and may cause TLS certificate issues.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is configured with an authorized time server
rules.explanation: Systemd-timesyncd should synchronize only with authorized NTP servers. Use of unauthorized servers can result in time manipulation.
rules.impact: Synchronization with an unauthorized NTP server allows an attacker to manipulate system time, which would break authentication, log correlation, and certificate operation.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: Using /etc/cron.allow (instead of /etc/cron.deny) implements a whitelist model for crontab. Only explicitly allowed users can create user cron jobs.
rules.impact: Without restricting access to crontab, any system user can create a regularly executed job. This increases the impact of any account compromise and makes monitoring more difficult.

rules.title: At is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at utility allows commands to be run at a specified time. Access to it must be restricted using /etc/at.allow as a whitelist, not /etc/at.deny.
rules.impact: Without restricting access to at, any user can schedule one-time execution of arbitrary commands. This increases the impact of compromise of any account on the system.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Bluetooth can be an attack vector, especially on servers.
rules.impact: Disabling Bluetooth reduces the likelihood of attack.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages can be used to redirect traffic to an attacker.
rules.impact: Accepting redirect packets allows traffic interception.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Even "secure" ICMP Redirect packets must not be accepted on servers that are not gateways.
rules.impact: Allowing secure-redirect enables route manipulation.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Some TCP/IP implementations generate responses to broadcast ICMP requests with incorrect error codes. Ignoring such responses protects against network scanning.
rules.impact: Without filtering spoofed ICMP replies, a server can be used to amplify attacks and network scanning. Incorrect ICMP messages may also disclose network topology information.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Responses to ICMP echo broadcast requests (Smurf attacks) can be used to amplify DDoS. Ignoring such requests prevents the server from participating in such attacks.
rules.impact: If the server responds to broadcast ICMP requests, an attacker can use it as an amplifier in a Smurf DDoS attack, generating traffic 500–1000 times the original.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: SYN cookies protect against SYN flood attacks.
rules.impact: Enabling SYN cookies prevents DoS attacks against the network stack.

rules.title: The auditd service is installed and running is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd package provides logging of user actions and system events for incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without auditing, attack sources and security policy violations cannot be identified.

rules.title: Systemctl enable rsyslog is active is configured
rules.explanation: The rsyslog service must be enabled to receive and write logs.
rules.impact: A disabled rsyslog daemon results in log loss.

rules.title: SSH access is configured
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups directives restrict which users are permitted SSH access. This implements the principle of least privilege for remote logon.
rules.impact: Without an explicit restriction, all system accounts, including service accounts, have SSH access. Compromise of any account provides a remote logon path and further persistence.

rules.title: The sshd banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH banner displays a warning before authentication.
rules.impact: A legal warning before logon may assist in legal proceedings.

rules.title: Sshd ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: Configure modern cryptographic algorithms for SSH.
rules.impact: Protection against outdated and insecure encryption algorithms.

rules.title: HostbasedAuthentication is disabled in SSH
rules.explanation: Host-based authentication trusts the remote host without verifying the user. This is an archaic and insecure method, fully superseded by key-based authentication.
rules.impact: Host-based authentication allows passwordless login to the server from trusted hosts. Compromise of any trusted host gives the attacker immediate access without additional authentication.

rules.title: The SSH IgnoreRhosts parameter is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter disables use of .rhosts and .shosts files for authentication. These are obsolete, unencrypted mechanisms that introduce serious vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: .rhosts files allow logon from a specified host without a password. An attacker who spoofs the IP address of a trusted host or compromises it will gain immediate access without authentication.

rules.title: Users must enter a password to elevate privileges is configured
rules.explanation: NOPASSWD in sudoers disables the password requirement when executing privileged commands. Such entries must be excluded because they violate the principle of identity confirmation.
rules.impact: Without a password requirement, an attacker who obtains access to a user session (terminal hijacking, a compromised SSH key) immediately obtains full root privileges without an additional barrier.

rules.title: Re-authentication on privilege elevation is not disabled globally is configured
rules.explanation: The global !authenticate flag in sudoers disables authentication for all users. This completely undermines the sudo security mechanism.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication means that any user can obtain root privileges without entering a password. Capture of any user session immediately results in full system compromise.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this will enable PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Lockout on failed logon attempts is configured (Automated)
rules.explanation: Configure login attempt limits.
rules.impact: Protects against brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: Unlock_time=n - Access will be re-enabled n seconds after lockout. A value of 0 has the same meaning as never - access will not be re-enabled without resetting faillock records using the faillock(8) command.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the effectiveness of brute-force password attacks against your systems.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts includes the root account is configured
rules.explanation: Even_deny_root - The root account can also be locked, like ordinary accounts. root_unlock_time=n - This option implies the even_deny_root option. Allows access to the root account after n seconds following lockout.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the effectiveness of brute-force password attacks against your systems.

rules.title: The number of changed characters in the password is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality difok option sets the number of characters in the new password that must not be present in the old password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise a password. Password complexity (or strength) is a measure of its effectiveness at resisting guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tested before the password is compromised.

rules.title: Password length is configured
rules.explanation: Minlen is the minimum allowed size of a new password (plus one if credits are not disabled, which is the default). It cannot be set below 6.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The number of identical consecutive characters in a password is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxrepeat option sets the maximum number of identical consecutive characters allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise a password. Password complexity (or strength) is a measure of its effectiveness at resisting guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tested before the password is compromised.

rules.title: The maximum number of consecutive characters in a password is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxsequence option sets the maximum length of monotonic character sequences in a new password. Examples of such a sequence are 12345 or fedcb. The check is disabled if the value is 0.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise a password. Password complexity (or strength) is a measure of its effectiveness at resisting guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tested before the password is compromised.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The pwquality dictcheck option determines whether words from the cracklib dictionary are checked.
rules.impact: If the operating system allows the user to choose passwords based on dictionary words, this increases the likelihood of password cracking, raising the chance of successful guessing and brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Password quality is applied for the root user is configured
rules.explanation: If the pwquality enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will return an error on a failed check even if the user changing the password is root. By default this option is disabled, which means a failed-check message is displayed, but root can still change the password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise a password. Password complexity (or strength) is a measure of its effectiveness at resisting guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tested before the password is compromised.

rules.title: The number of remembered passwords (password history) is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be checked to ensure that users do not reuse recent passwords. The number of remembered passwords is set via the remember argument value specified for the pam_pwhistory module. remember=<N> - <N> is the number of old passwords to remember.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: Password history is applied for the root user is configured
rules.explanation: If the pwhistory enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will also enforce password history for the root user.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes the use_authtok parameter is configured
rules.explanation: Use_authtok - When changing a password, forces the module to set the new password to the one previously provided by a stacked password module.
rules.impact: Use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include the nullok parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default pam_unix.so behavior of denying user access to a service when the official password is empty.
rules.impact: Using a strong password is necessary to protect personal and confidential information from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include the remember parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The remember=n argument stores the last n passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd to enforce password change history and prevent a user from switching between the same passwords too frequently. The MD5 password hashing algorithm is used to store old passwords. The pam_pwhistory module should be used instead of this option. The pam_pwhistory module stores the last n passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd using the password hashing algorithm set in the pam_unix module. This allows the sha512 hashing algorithm to be used.
rules.impact: The remember=n argument should be removed to ensure that a strong password hashing algorithm is used. A stronger hash provides additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine old local user passwords stored in /etc/security/opasswd.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: A cryptographic hash function transforms input of arbitrary length into output of fixed length. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password, converting the password into another string called the hashed password.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 and yescrypt algorithms provide a stronger hash than other algorithms used by Linux to generate password hashes. A stronger hash provides additional system protection by increasing the level of effort required for an attacker to successfully determine local user passwords.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes the use_authtok parameter is configured
rules.explanation: Use_authtok - When changing a password, forces the module to set the new password to the one previously provided by a stacked password module.
rules.impact: Use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: The minimum password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The minimum password age defines the number of days a password must be used before it can be changed. PASS_MIN_DAYS <N> is the minimum number of days allowed between password changes. Any attempt to change the password before this time will be rejected. If not specified, 0 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe the chosen password is protected against compromise. Unfortunately, passwords are compromised, and if an attacker targets a specific individual user's account, then, with prior knowledge about that user, reuse of old, potentially compromised passwords may lead to a security breach. By restricting how frequently a password can be changed, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0 is configured
rules.explanation: GID (Group ID) 0 belongs to the root group. Ensure that no other accounts use GID 0.
rules.impact: The presence of other accounts with GID 0 can lead to privilege escalation, as such accounts will have the same rights as root.

rules.title: The root group is the only group with GID 0 is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that only the root group has GID 0.
rules.impact: The presence of other groups with GID 0 may result in unauthorized access to system resources.

rules.title: The root password is set is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that a password is set for the root account.
rules.impact: Absence of a root password leaves the system vulnerable to unauthorized access.

rules.title: The root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the umask for the root user is set to a secure value (for example, 027 or 077).
rules.impact: A correctly configured umask restricts permissions on files created by root.
rules.scope: Files /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, or the root user shell settings.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell is configured
rules.explanation: System accounts (for example, bin, daemon) must not have a valid login shell (for example, /bin/bash).
rules.impact: This prevents system accounts from being used to log on.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked is configured
rules.explanation: Accounts without a valid login shell (for example, /sbin/nologin) must be locked.
rules.impact: This prevents such accounts from being used to log in.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that /sbin/nologin or /usr/sbin/nologin is not present in /etc/shells.
rules.impact: This prevents nologin from being used as a valid login shell.

rules.title: Permissions are 644 and the owner is root:root is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd must be readable by all, but writable only by root.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow modification of system credentials.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd service must be running continuously and enabled at boot. Stopping it interrupts collection of critical kernel-level security events.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd leaves the system without kernel auditing. All attacker actions after the service is stopped (file changes, privilege use, network connections) will remain unrecorded.

rules.title: Auditing of processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter audit=1 enables auditing at the earliest stages of boot, before auditd starts. This ensures capture of bootloader and system initialization events.
rules.impact: Without audit=1 in kernel parameters, early boot events (init, systemd) are not recorded. An attacker who injected code into the initialization process would remain invisible to the audit system.

rules.title: The audit backlog limit is sufficient is configured
rules.explanation: Audit_backlog_limit determines the size of the kernel audit event queue. A value of ≥8192 prevents event loss under high load and ensures audit completeness.
rules.impact: A small backlog_limit leads to loss of audit events under high load. An attacker can deliberately create load to overflow the queue and conceal their actions in the audit log.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-remote package is installed if remote log forwarding is required.
rules.impact: Systemd-journal-remote allows logs to be sent to a remote server for centralized collection, which improves security and manageability.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload authentication is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that authentication for systemd-journal-upload (sending logs to a remote server) is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring authentication prevents unauthorized submission of logs or submission to spoofed servers.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-upload service is enabled and active when remote log forwarding is used.
rules.impact: Enabling the service is required to actually send logs to the remote host.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-remote service (for receiving logs from remote hosts) is not used if it is not needed.
rules.impact: If the system is not intended to receive remote logs, disabling this service reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically is configured
rules.explanation: Max_log_file_action=keep_logs prevents automatic deletion of old audit logs. Logs should be archived or rotated, but not destroyed automatically.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs destroys evidence of past incidents. An attacker who remains undetected benefits from traces of their activity disappearing after some time.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from remote clients is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog must not accept logs over the network (imtcp/imudp) unless the server is a centralized log collector. Accepting inbound logs expands the attack surface.
rules.impact: Active reception of UDP/TCP logs opens a network port for inbound connections. This is a vector for injecting forged log records and DoS via log overflow from external sources.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Auditing unsuccessful file open attempts (EACCES, EPERM) helps detect filesystem reconnaissance and attempts at unauthorized access to protected data.
rules.impact: A series of file access denials is a clear sign of reconnaissance or an attempt to bypass restrictions. Without auditing such events, an attacker can systematically enumerate accessible files without detection.

rules.title: Audit log file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: Auditd log files should have permissions of no more than 0600 (root only). This prevents unprivileged users from reading critical security events.
rules.impact: Readable audit logs disclose to unprivileged users details of system events, security configuration, and user behavior patterns, which are used to plan attacks.

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs have insufficient space is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the system warns when audit logs have insufficient space.
rules.impact: Timely warnings about insufficient space allow administrators to take action before the system stops recording audit events, which could result in the loss of critical security information.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded.
rules.impact: Ensure that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded.
rules.impact: Ensure that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded.
rules.impact: Ensure that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded.
rules.impact: Ensure that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded.

rules.title: The running configuration and the on-disk configuration are the same is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the running configuration and the on-disk configuration are the same.
rules.impact: Ensure that the running configuration and the on-disk configuration are the same.

rules.title: The audit log file mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and its activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records may disclose system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising their confidentiality.
rules.scope: Audit log directory permission settings (from auditd.conf)

rules.title: The owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and its activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records may disclose system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising their confidentiality.
rules.scope: Audit log file permission settings (in the directory from auditd.conf)

rules.title: The group owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the group owner of audit log files is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that the group owner of audit log files is configured.
rules.scope: Owner settings for audit log files

rules.title: The audit log file directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the audit log file directory mode is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that the audit log file directory mode is configured.

rules.title: Audit configuration file mode is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that audit configuration file mode is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that audit configuration file mode is configured.
rules.scope: Permission parameters for .conf and .rules files in /etc/audit/

rules.title: The owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the owner of audit configuration files is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that the owner of audit configuration files is configured.
rules.scope: Parameters for owner of .conf and .rules files in /etc/audit/

rules.title: The group owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that the group owner of audit configuration files is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that the group owner of audit configuration files is configured.
rules.scope: Group owner parameters for .conf and .rules files in /etc/audit/

rules.title: The audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open-source audit tools required to successfully view and manage audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting tools used to view and manage log data. Protection of audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operations on audit information.
rules.scope: Permission settings for the auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, and augenrules files

rules.explanation: Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open-source audit tools required to successfully view and manage audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting tools used to view and manage log data. Protection of audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operations on audit information.
rules.scope: Owner parameters for audit utilities (auditctl and others)

rules.explanation: This check verifies that the group owner of audit tools is configured.
rules.impact: Ensure that the group owner of audit tools is configured.
rules.scope: Group owner parameters for audit utilities (auditctl and others)

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured correctly
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow contains group password hashes and the list of group administrators. Permissions 000 or 640:root:shadow prevent unauthorized access to this information.
rules.impact: A readable /etc/gshadow exposes group passwords and lists of privileged members. This information allows an attacker to join password-protected groups without authorization.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured correctly
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow- is a backup of /etc/gshadow containing group passwords. It requires equivalent protection. Weak permissions on the backup negate protection of the primary file.
rules.impact: A gshadow backup file with more permissive permissions becomes a bypass path for obtaining group passwords. An attacker may prefer to attack the backup rather than the strictly protected primary file.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that /etc/shells has permissions 644 and is owned by root:root.
rules.impact: This prevents unauthorized modification of the list of allowed shells.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/security/opasswd are configured
rules.explanation: This check verifies that /etc/security/opasswd has permissions 600 and is owned by root:root.
rules.impact: This protects password history from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured correctly
rules.explanation: All interactive users must have existing home directories. Absence of a home directory can lead to unpredictable application behavior and storage of files in undesirable locations.
rules.impact: A user without a home directory may create files in the current working directory (/, /tmp). This can result in files being created in system directories or in conflicts with other users.
